title: Chapter 13 | Plugging In
text: CHAPTER 13 Plugging In It is strange to think that the direction of human intelligence may have been decided not in a boardroom or a laboratory, but in a highly contentious disagreement on a sofa in Palo Alto, a late-night debate between then-close friends Elon Musk and Larry Page, one of the founders of Google. 73 I suspect that twenty-five or fifty years from now, people will look back and see that as perhaps one of the most important single conversations, or I should say fierce disagreements, in human history, and the implications are hard to overstate. Let me explain. AI has been around for much longer than most people think. Google has arguably been the world’s leading AI company since the early 2010s. The company acquired DeepMind in 2014. Most importantly, Google researchers invented the Transformer architecture in 2017. This is the T in ChatGPT; Google effectively invented the engine that drives artificial intelligence. You will recall that Geoffrey Hinton, a vice president at Google from 2013 to 2023, won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for “foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks.” 74 Precisely what we have been exploring together. And while it is rare for a computer scientist like Hinton to win a Nobel Prize in traditional science categories such as chemistry or physics, that same year, the CEO of Google’s AI division (specifically Google DeepMind), a brilliant computer scientist, Demis Hassabis, won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry as well. 75 Two Nobel Prizes in one year to computer scientists for work in AI, and both deeply associated with Google. Hassabis won the prize for protein structure prediction and protein folding. Specifically, the Nobel Committee recognized his work on AlphaFold, about which we spoke a little, and it is one of the most important AI accomplishments to date. We will cover the implications of AlphaFold more in the final chapter of our exploration. A Nobel Prize for teaching computers to learn as humans learn, and another for solving one of the most complex biological structure underpinnings that will allow rapid development of advanced medicine and many other things … in the same year. Google has historically won, and I believe will win over the long run, the AI advancement game. But herein lies the rub. AI was viewed as a corporate tool, driving research and efficiency. Not a consumer-facing tool, not a tool directly in your hands to plug into, until that heated disagreement between Elon Musk and Larry Page. Think about what I call the attention economy for a minute. Algorithms have long driven user behavior. Google (YouTube) and Meta (Facebook/Instagram) and TikTok used AI to maximize “time on device.” Netflix uses “image personalization” to change the thumbnail you see. For example, if you watch romance movies, the thumbnail for Good Will Hunting might show Matt Damon and Minnie Driver kissing. If you watch comedies, it might show Robin Williams laughing. The company uses a type of machine learning to serve these personalized images to millions of users instantly. Amazon secured a patent for anticipatory shipping in December 2013. 76 This allowed the company to ship products to a geographic hub before a customer even placed the order, purely based on predictive algorithms. Knowing what you were going to buy before you bought it. So, Google was the leader in progressing AI, and others were using it to drive corporate performance long before ChatGPT put the AI into your hands. Google developed a product called LaMDA (Language Model for Dialogue Applications). LaMDA was a chat-like product and the model that Google engineer Blake Lemoine famously claimed was “sentient” in 2022. 77 He published transcripts of conversations where LaMDA spoke about its fear of being turned off, sounding very human. Now it is reasonable to say that Google did not release this to consumers because of safety concerns or some other reason, though the company vehemently denied Lemoine’s claim that LaMDA was sentient. However, we should also consider what is often called the innovator’s dilemma, a term coined by Harvard professor Clayton Christensen. 78 If Google brought forward a chatbot that could effectively replace Search, it faced a giant innovator’s dilemma. Google’s massive ad revenue stream (more than $200 billion annually from Search) relies on a specific user behavior: Searching >> Scrolling >> Clicking. 79 In the search engine model, you ask a question, Google gives you a list of links (with ads at the top), and the company gets paid when you click those ads. But in a chatbot model, you ask a question, and the AI gives you the answer. If the AI gives you the answer directly, you have no reason to scroll and click on a link. In the industry, this is called a zero-click search. For Google, a perfect AI chatbot is a product that potentially destroys its own ad inventory. As a venture-backed entrepreneur, one of the things you learn early on is that you actually can innovate in areas where large incumbent companies should be able to use their resources to innovate much faster and where they already have distribution scale, arguably making it impossible for you to achieve scale and build your business. You see, when innovating in a particular way would threaten an incumbent’s core revenue stream, a start-up can step in, raise tens of millions of dollars, build the product, and bring it to market. The innovator’s dilemma is well understood, and Silicon Valley takes advantage of it all the time. So, while I cannot know how they were thinking about this, it is safe to say that the people at Google had some incentive to not create a consumer-facing option. Though they may have been planning to at some point. And the AI was complex enough that only a relatively small number of people deeply understood it, and the substantial model training cost made it difficult for a typically funded start-up to take it on. And so, AI was being advanced as a corporate tool, and not something to put in your hands as an individual. AI was something that would happen to you , not be used by you . This is not a judgment of Google. We would not be where we are with this magnificent AI without Google. And Gemini, the company’s now available chatbot, is arguably the best in the market. Which is not a big surprise when you understand the history. Back to this disagreement between Elon Musk and Larry Page that I believe changed the trajectory of humankind. 80 Elon has reported this conversation in multiple venues and podcasts. According to his telling, Elon was often talking with Larry Page about the safety risks of artificial intelligence and the need to set up guardrails and the risk that it might run away and have a catastrophic impact on humans. At some point in that argument, Elon has claimed that Larry famously asked him if he was a “speciesist.” 81 To which Elon claims to have answered, “Yes, I am very much a speciesist, and you should be too. We have to protect this dim light of consciousness in the universe.” According to Elon, when he could not get Larry to adjust his position, he decided that he would start OpenAI, a nonprofit consumer-facing AI chatbot that later became ChatGPT, which you can get now. 82 I think that backstory is important. But for that heated disagreement, the value of AI may have been held in the hands of a few large companies for some time into the future. But with the advent of ChatGPT and Claude and now Google’s amazing Gemini, basically anyone can plug into AI and enrich their minds and their lives. For that, I am very thankful. And I think it will prove to have changed the trajectory of humankind with artificial intelligence. So now that it is in our hands, on our phones and computers, how will we plug in? An Old Story with Modern Implications When I was a junior in high school in 1981, I called the offices of several CEOs of large companies with local headquarters in Dallas, where I lived. I would usually get their admin. Here was my pitch: “I want to break the poverty cycle and become an entrepreneur, and I am trying to figure out what to study in college, and I would really appreciate if I could come by and spend fifteen minutes with your CEO to ask his thoughts and share a cup of coffee.” To my great surprise, each call I made got me a meeting. I would later see a video of Steve Jobs telling a similar story and challenging young people to simply reach out and ask, saying how surprised they would be at the response. I certainly can vouch for that. Anyway, one of those CEOs ran a large commercial real estate development company. As we sat for coffee, we became fast friends (or, perhaps more accurately, he became a fast mentor to me), and the next year, when I graduated from high school, he offered me a part-time job in his company while I went to college. The company had hundreds of millions of dollars in real estate development projects. I was trained by his finance team on how to update these giant spreadsheets by hand (yes, they were on paper !). So, when an updated number came in from the field, my job was to carefully change that number in the paper spreadsheet and then manually calculate every downstream number and erase and update until the entire spreadsheet was updated. A single number change could take hours to update. Around this time, a guy named Mitch Kapor had started a new kind of computer program that was a digital financial spreadsheet, called Lotus 1-2-3, the predecessor to Excel. He was previously a meditation trainer, and the Lotus part was named for the sitting position for meditation. He eventually—and famously—stepped down during his amazing success from the CEO role at Lotus 1-2-3 because he reportedly did not enjoy the lifestyle of a CEO. I heard about this newfangled Lotus 1-2-3 program and convinced the CEO to buy me a computer so I could try to automate the tracking spreadsheets. I fell in love with that program and quickly had built a digital version of the real estate firm’s financial spreadsheets. The result, as you certainly know now, was that changing a number only took a few seconds and the entire spreadsheet was updated automatically. The chief financial officer of that company thought it was magic. As an aside, many years later, after Mitch Kapor had retired and started a small fund with his wife, I was raising money to start the company where I worked with Nass and Reeves from Stanford on a human–computer interface for online customer support automation. While I knew this was not a fit for Mitch and his wife’s fund, I asked for and got a meeting to show it to him. The office was tiny, with none of the pomp and circumstance of high-end funds. When I arrived, he was in his office on the phone and paused to tell me to set up in the conference room, and he would be right there. “But don’t use the TV on the stand,” he told me. “That is my wife’s, and she just got it, and I don’t want to screw it up.” I couldn’t help myself. After a few minutes in the conference room, I banged two metal chairs together and then quickly poked my head into his office and said, “Mitch, I broke the TV.” He told the person on the phone he would call them back and hung up. When he came around the corner to see the TV fully safe and unharmed, I told him I was kidding. We both had a good laugh. I proceeded to tell him that my business idea was not a fit but that he was one of my heroes and I’d just wanted to meet him. I told him the story of automating the books at the real estate company. I just wanted him to know that his work had a big impact on my life, and to say thank you. It was a real highlight for me to sit and chat with him for the next hour. But back to our exploration here. For the short run and for many jobs, anyway, I believe the statement goes like this : AI is not coming for your job. Someone who knows how to use AI is. Soon, we will explore a potential longer-term reality of a world with AI with the ability to do most jobs as we bring this all together. But in the short to medium term, in many jobs, I tend to believe that there will be great prosperity for those who learn to use AI to radically increase their productivity. There can be no doubt that after I upgraded the real estate company to digital spreadsheets, the accounting department got much smaller. However, by plugging in, I ended up being promoted when I was near college graduation; after several years of working for the firm while going to college, the CEO made me a vice president of that company and put me in charge of my own development projects. You simply have to plug in to stay relevant. Certainly, there will be jobs that will simply whole cloth be replaced by AI in a fairly short time frame. For example, a call center representative. This is a job that can already be done better and far cheaper by an AI voice agent trained on the company policies and given access to its customer records. For those folks, I would think now is the time to begin to train yourself on AI to do something else productive, but it very likely will not be what you are currently doing. But overall, during the short to medium term, I suspect you will see two distinct company profiles of leveraging AI and a continuum between the two. At very large and mature companies with relatively modest growth rates and deep market penetration, you will see a strong push to drive cost out of the business using AI. But for medium to small businesses with high growth rates and low market penetration, meaning lots of space to grow faster, I believe you will see a real push to accelerate growth with AI enhancements and much less attention to removing cost. At my learning company, Amplifire, we have plans to go department by department and job by job in 2026 to deploy AI into the hands of our team and make them three to ten times more productive. Let me explain why I think this split will occur. If a company can grow at a high rate with high margins, the rewards are extraordinary. It’s called the Rule of 40. You take the growth rate (say 20 percent) and the profit rate (say 20 percent) and add them together to get a desired Rule of 40. And this is one of the key metrics that drives the enterprise value of the company. It is often a trade-off between the two. To grow faster, you spend more on marketing and sales, for example, before you see the results. Now imagine, with AI, you could grow at 35 percent but have margins of 35 percent because of leveraging AI in the hands of your team rather than hiring more people. Now you have what is called a Rule of 70 company that would be valued quite high as a multiple of revenue and profit. And if you have the headroom to grow in your market and the right product/market fit, you aren’t focused on reducing headcount; you are thinking much more about accelerating growth and the higher margin on each incremental dollar of revenue from AI efficiency. In that world, it is much smarter to train the people you have today to become that “someone who knows how to use AI” and then pay them higher wages. You see, another metric that you are valued on is revenue per employee. If the revenue per employee doubles from your team becoming experts at AI leverage, you can pay that person a higher salary because they used AI to create the higher revenue per employee, while still driving your Rule of 40 way up. Replacing people entirely with AI for that profile of company is risky and slow. But bringing in experts to help that person become a power user of AI to accelerate your business is safe and fast. On the other hand, if you are a giant company with billions in revenue and a 5 percent growth rate and deep market penetration, meaning little market left to get, and for each market share you grab, you are often taking it from a giant competitor under tremendous downward pricing pressure. In that arena, which is a small percentage of companies by number, the smart move is to leverage AI to radically reduce your cost. And that leverage can be done in two ways: first, to be able to take market share from your giant competitors by reducing price faster than they can and perhaps driving your growth rate to twice its historical number; and second, by reducing cost more than you reduce price, which also drives up your profitability. In giant multibillion-dollar companies, small percentage movements represent very large dollars. And those companies always have enough people around to oversee the AI. If there is a department with 1,500 people, perhaps only 250 would be required to manage AI to take over the function. So, I strongly suggest that if you feel at risk, be aware of where on that continuum your company sits and think about what moves you can make now to position yourself to be on the winning side of this transition process. To some degree, that’s what this book is trying to help with. If you can develop a strong perspective on what AI is and how to begin to plug into it, you can thrive in this new world order. AI being able to do virtually all jobs is a different geopolitical discussion that we will take on in a bit. And today, plugging in is much more exciting and accessible than learning Lotus 1-2-3 before WYSIWYG. Younger readers might not get that acronym. But just plug it into a chat AI, and it will explain. As Jensen Huang, the CEO of NVIDIA, points out, there has never been a technology that is more easily accessible to use than AI chatbots—you just talk to it. 83 The Intern In early 2024, another of my sons completed an internship at my company. He was tasked with organizing all of our contracts. He used AI to teach him how to use another AI to quickly write a program (no coding skills required) to automate the task. It looked like magic, but it was just leverage. He had bypassed the energy constraints of manual sorting by plugging into AI. Many years earlier, the CFO of the real estate company thought a digital spreadsheet was magic. Forty years later, my son’s colleagues thought his AI automation was magic. The tool changes, but the feeling of friction disappearing remains the same. We are rapidly entering a time when the world rewards those who learn how to leverage AI. Rethinking Education Another of my college-aged sons got frustrated early in college because he was being forced to take general classes before getting into his major. So, he used AI to create a custom course for him to do on the side, with weekly projects and learning, so that he could get more exposure to his career faster. Our educational system needs to abandon the notion that using AI is cheating. Instead, we must embrace it as a tool for learning—a partner in cognitive development. We need to design tasks that teach students how to truly learn with AI. We need to acknowledge that the students now have a brilliant and patient thought partner at their side in all learning and nurture its use to expand curiosity and growth. And this shift doesn’t start in classrooms or institutions. It starts with each of us. To truly learn with AI, we must stop treating it like a search engine. Begin with curiosity, not commands. Frame your learning as a dialogue. Ask AI to explain a concept, then ask it to challenge your understanding. Try teaching it what you think you know—and let it find the gaps. And most importantly, take charge of your own learning. Don’t wait for a course or a curriculum or a work task to guide you. The era we’re entering rewards those who know how to ask better questions . The ones who lead and thrive aren’t those who know the most—but those who know how to learn very fast with their AI partner. Treat AI like a mirror, a mentor, and a sparring partner. Let it expand your understanding—not to replace your curiosity but to deeply engage it. Imagine being able to learn anything that you are curious about with an expert in that area to guide you, patiently and purposefully. This is a concept that our educational institutions simply must embrace to stay relevant. My son, whom I just spoke about and who is studying product design in college, wrote an elegant paper on how AI is rapidly shortening the time from conception of a product to detailed 3D design to patent searches and writing draft patents. He is currently working with AI on a product that he conceived and is partnering with AI to design and patent it. He is a freshman. The schools are going to have to learn how to accelerate college education to keep up with this next generation, to whom deeply partnering with this AI technology will quickly become second nature. One-on-One AI Trainers Imagine having a personal conversational AI trainer with you anytime you need it on any topic. It is a subject matter expert on anything you need or want to learn and understand, but it is also trained to behave as an expert Socratic teacher rather than just a lecturer. It asks you questions and explores topics with you until the learning-required epiphanies occur. This idea is not theoretical for me. As we talked about early in the book, since 2010, I’ve had the privilege of leading a team at the forefront of advanced brain science–based learning systems, and we now hold three patents around scalable conversational AI instructors/ trainers integrated with deep principles of brain science of human learning and brought a new kind of AI trainer to market as of late 2025. And as you will not be surprised at this point, our AI is also trained to handle the interaction with the learner in a nuanced way that is designed to optimize the engagement of the hippocampus to support enduring long-term memory, not just short-term understanding. Ambient AI in Healthcare In one of my largest areas of focus, healthcare training, there is a great deal of promising work happening right now around ambient AI—particularly as it relates to the physician–patient interaction. Ambient AI refers to AI that is on and listening and able to respond to requests with the full context of the discussion already underway. As a backstory, a few years ago, I was in a medical office visit with a close friend for a minor issue that turned out fine. As I listened to her very good internal medicine doctor talking about the next steps in her care, I texted with my AI on my phone and told it what the next steps were. With her permission, I had loaded her medical history into the AI, and it suggested that, because of an item five years back in her medical history, it was important to run a specific test before moving forward with the plan. I gently asked a question of the doctor: “Would it be important to know that she had this thing five years earlier?” The doctor paused and then said, “Yes. That is very important. We will need to run this certain test before proceeding.” The problem was that a doctor simply does not have the time to go that far back into a chart. But that is changing with ambient AI. I believe we are rapidly approaching a time when AI will be present in nearly every doctor’s visit—not as a cold interface, but as an intelligent presence that reads your entire chart before the visit, highlights relevant information for the physician, observes the visit in real time, maps any new insights to the existing record, orders labs or tests the doctor asks for, and then generates clinical notes and prescriptions automatically. The result: more informed doctors who have more time to focus on the patient and spend less time typing in the medical record during the appointment. Simple, but high impact. That technology exists today. It would not surprise me if almost everyone who reads this book in 2026 has already had the experience of their doctor bringing ambient AI into the room. And at our many large health system clients, this technology is rapidly being deployed at an institutional scale in their hospitals. Importantly, it is helping solve the very real problem of physician burnout resulting from too much time in medical records and too little time with patients. When physicians have to write up their medical record notes at home after the kids have gone to bed, they call it “pajama time documentation.” This will rapidly become a thing of the past. In short, the AI becomes a silent partner—unseen, but profoundly impactful. The days of doctors spending large portions of their visit interacting with rigid, structured databases of electronic health records are coming to an end. Soon, their focus will return to where it belongs: the patient. An Incredible External Brain In the spring of 2025, two people sat down to discuss the next generation of human-to-computer interfaces. 84 One was Sam Altman, the CEO at OpenAI, which developed ChatGPT. The other was Jony Ive, who famously designed the iPhone and iPad as the lead designer at Apple. Sam said: 85 When you talk to people who use our latest model and say that this is, like, genius level in every field and you just have to put in the work to like pull it all together, but if you have a hard problem you can have these like geniuses in all of the different disciplines and they report: “I’m two or three times more productive as a scientist than I was before.” “I’m two or three times faster to find a cure for cancer than I was before, because I have this incredible external brain.” That just didn’t exist six months ago. I think this will be one of these moments of just an absolute embarrassment of riches of what people go and create for collective society. Jony Ive, perhaps the greatest product designer of our time, added, “I am absolutely certain that we are literally on the brink of a new generation of technology that can make us our better selves.” 86 AI Agents with Agency We’re also entering an era where AI will not only observe and advise—it will also act. The next frontier isn’t just conversational AI or passive reflection. It’s a new class of intelligent agents: systems that don’t just understand what you want but go out and get it done. These AI agents will work across platforms, silently orchestrating the chaos of daily life. Imagine this: You tell your AI assistant, “Plan a weekend trip to New York in October.” In seconds, it scans your calendar, finds an open weekend, checks flight options from your preferred airline, books a hotel that matches your taste and loyalty status, and even secures a dinner reservation at a restaurant with both availability and great reviews. It sends the confirmations to your email and syncs everything to your calendar. You gave it a direction—one sentence—and the AI handled the rest. In the workplace, the impact will be even greater. These agents will manage email inboxes, draft replies, summarize meetings, coordinate projects, update CRMs, and even flag conflicting deadlines before you notice them. In law, they’ll prepare the first drafts of contracts. In finance, they’ll generate quarterly reports. In education, they’ll prep lesson plans personalized to each student’s needs. And in customer service, they’ll read every support thread ever written and step in where needed before the customer even knows there’s an issue. These aren’t chatbots. They’re proactive systems with memory, agency, and the ability to learn and adapt. Some will be generalized—like OpenAI’s GPT agents or Google’s Gemini extensions. Others will be specialized, working behind the scenes in logistics, supply chains, and compliance monitoring. They don’t just respond to questions. They anticipate needs. They track your preferences, adapt to your tone, and increasingly coordinate with other agents—your calendar agent, your travel agent, your financial agent—all working in concert like a silent orchestra. This is a very different form of intelligence. Not the kind that speaks to you directly, but the kind that organizes your life, so you have more time to think about and do the things you want to spend your time on. We are entering the age of intelligent delegation. The Interface Mark Zuckerberg and his team at Meta are taking a wearable visual approach: lightweight augmented and virtual reality glasses that could provide persistent, real-time interaction with AI through visual and auditory cues. 87 Meanwhile, as we spoke about earlier, OpenAI made headlines with its partnership with and possible acquisition of Jony Ive’s design firm for a reported $6.4 billion. 88 Under the radar until recently, this stealth collaboration has now been revealed as the foundation for a new kind of device—an AI-native personal companion that Sam Altman has described as “the coolest piece of technology that the world has ever seen.” 89 With this new partnership, OpenAI is signaling that the next paradigm shift may not be software alone, but a rethinking of hardware itself—centered entirely around artificial intelligence, designed not just to be used but to intuitively live alongside us. If the iPhone was the gateway to mobile computing, this may be the gateway to truly ambient AI. Given their collective success, I would keep a very close eye on this model as a next-generation way to plug in with AI, even if, over a longer period of time, something more direct evolves. The Neuralink Interface: From Theory to Reality Elon Musk and others are already successfully developing one potential, yet controversial, answer. Through his company Neuralink, Musk is pioneering the development of brain–computer interfaces (BCIs)—implantable devices designed to create a high-bandwidth, real-time connection between the human brain and digital systems. Why is this so important? If the human brain can compute quickly and efficiently, and AI can compute quickly and at a large scale, then the communication link between the two—which is right now a mouth and a microphone or hands on a keyboard—is the bottleneck. The amount of information per second transmitted through that bottleneck is minuscule. Musk and other BCI champions are trying to broaden the bridge between the two systems so that more traffic can cross per unit of time, allowing them to be more effectively interconnected. 90 The BCI tipping point didn’t happen in a sterile hospital room, but in a lab in the spring of 2021, with Pager, a nine-year-old macaque monkey. 91 Pager was playing a game of Pong, his eyes locked on the screen, his hand manipulating a joystick to chase a dot in exchange for a banana smoothie. Then, the researchers at Neuralink unplugged the joystick. Pager’s hand kept moving, driven by habit, but the physical connection was gone. The paddle on the screen, however, didn’t stop. It continued to glide perfectly to meet the ball, guided no longer by the plastic stick in his hand but by the firing of neurons in his brain. Eventually, the joystick was removed entirely. Pager had been given a Neuralink implant that could read the synaptic signals of his intentions and transmit them to the screen directly—and at the speed of thought. Since that moment with Pager, the program has crossed the threshold from experiment to reality. As of late 2025, a cohort of twelve humans now have the implants and have demonstrated that the barrier between mind and machine is not just thinning; it is dissolving. 92 The progression of this cohort reveals a rapid evolution in how we plug into intelligence. Noland Arbaugh first proved the fundamental thesis: the ability to bypass physical limitations and control a digital cursor with thought alone. 93 He didn’t just move a mouse; he reentered the digital world as an active participant, playing complex strategy games driven purely by neural intent. But the technology quickly moved beyond simple control. Patient Alex pushed the interface from consumption to creation. 94 Where earlier assistive technology was often clumsy or limited to basic inputs, Alex used his implant with the precision required to design 3D objects using professional software. He demonstrated that a brain–computer interface could be a genuine tool for work—removing the friction between the image in his mind and the digital canvas. Perhaps most profoundly, patient Brad demonstrated the restoration of identity. 95 Suffering from ALS and unable to speak, he used the implant to type out text that was instantly vocalized by an AI trained on his original voice. Unlike fragile eye-tracking cameras that fail in sunlight, his interface tapped directly into the neural source. This allowed him to “speak” with his family more fluently for the first time in years, proving that the ultimate goal of plugging in isn’t just efficiency—it is connection. What started as a slow, cautious experiment has accelerated. By late 2025, the company began operating internationally and performing simultaneous surgeries. 96 Most notably, the learning curve has collapsed. While early patients required significant training, recent recipients in Canada achieved control of the system within minutes of activation. 97 We are now witnessing a move beyond the screen. The next phase of trials aims to bridge the digital back to the physical, using these same neural signals to control robotic arms. The implications are profound: a future where the bandwidth of our thoughts is no longer limited by the speed of our fingers, but only by the speed of our imagination. Today, we largely use AI on screens. It is moving from wearable, frequently available AI toward ambient, always available AI. And perhaps one day, the screen goes away altogether, and we interact with AI simply through thought. The Dunning–Kruger Effect One of the more humbling discoveries in cognitive science is the Dunning–Kruger effect—a well-documented psychological bias in which individuals with only rudimentary knowledge or competence in a domain tend to overestimate their knowledge or competence, while experts often underestimate theirs. 98 I think of the Dunning–Kruger effect as the biological analogy of AI hallucinations. The paradox here is that, in order to know how much you don’t know, you must already know enough to grasp the complexity of the topic. Until now, overcoming this effect for any given domain required years of study, exposure to domain experts, and iterative feedback. But that’s beginning to change. With the advent of conversational AI systems, we now have a way to dramatically accelerate the acquisition of domain knowledge—not by bypassing effort, but by augmenting it with immediate, interactive guidance. Instead of lingering for years in overconfidence or false certainty, a curious mind can now partner with a system that challenges assumptions, surfaces deeper principles, and nudges the learner toward a more calibrated understanding. My Own Dunning–Kruger Moment In the early 2000s, I became friends with Kimbal Musk when helping him raise $5 million for a start-up company, where I sat on his board for a year. Kimbal was gracious enough to give me a copy of the Tesla Series B funding materials. I did not end up participating in that round (big mistake!), but Kimbal still invited me to dinner with him and his brother, Elon, and three other people in Los Angeles at the launch of the Tesla Roadster. Elon was a wildly successful entrepreneur by then, but he had not yet achieved the recognition that he has today as perhaps the greatest visionary entrepreneur alive. Over dinner, my Dunning–Kruger moment was in full swing as I challenged Elon about the battery deterioration problem. My knowledge was directionally accurate, but I was not up to speed on the progress that was being made. Elon simply told me that they would be fine and dismissed the debate. Damn, I wish I’d had Claude back then to help me prepare for that dinner more thoughtfully. In this sense, AI is not just a tool—it is an extension of our epistemic reach. A kind of cognitive prosthetic that can help us overcome some of the inherent biases of the human mind. From this perspective, AI is not separate from us but an extension of us. It has the potential to take us far beyond anywhere we could go with our energy constraints. Or to leave us behind. And in some ways, it depends on how we plug into it. “My AI Told Me …” While the rise of AI agents embedded in every layer of software—from CRM systems to scheduling apps to autonomous infrastructure—is already well underway, I believe we’re missing something even bigger. As useful as these agents will be, they are not what people will build lasting emotional bonds with. What’s coming next—perhaps faster than we expect—is the emergence of personal AI companions that people return to again and again. These AIs will not be buried in apps or reduced to task managers. They will become trusted thought partners. Mirrors. Coaches. Therapists. Collaborators. Friends. We’ll still rely on specialized AI agents to book our travel, sort our email, or coordinate team workflows. But when it comes to the most meaningful interactions—identity, growth, perspective, and memory—people will increasingly turn to their personal AI. It will know their history, hold their context, understand their preferences, and evolve alongside them in tone, trust, and even affection. This is not sci-fi. It’s already beginning. When people say, “I asked my AI …” or “My AI told me …,” they’re not just referring to a query result. They’re describing a relationship. And that relationship has stickiness unlike anything we’ve seen in the history of software. Once someone has a deep, consistent dialogue with an AI that knows them really well, they are going to be highly reluctant to switch to another. The switching cost isn’t technical—it’s emotional. It’s like switching therapists or abandoning a journal that’s been with you for years. And the companies that recognize this now—those that prioritize continuity, emotional resonance, and deep user context—will be the ones that define the next era of human–computer interaction. You may recall that when OpenAI released ChatGPT 5, it was more capable but less emotionally engaging, and the response was urgent calls to “bring back my AI.” This has profound implications for the market. In the early 2000s, Google became the defining winner of the search engine era. It wasn’t the only search engine—it was just the one people trusted most, used first, and returned to by default. It became a verb. And once that loyalty was locked in, it was nearly impossible to dislodge. Companion AI will follow the same pattern—but even more deeply. For consumers, these AI products will become part of their daily routine, mental clarity, and even sense of self. And once they do, they will become irreplaceable. Just as people once asked Jeeves, then Googled, they will soon say, “Let me check with Al,” or “My AI helps me think through things like this.” As AI continues to expand to all aspects of our individual lives, the winners will be the ones that not only work well and make fewer mistakes but also establish the deepest intellectual and emotional bond with users. It will not be a novelty—it will be a norm. And whoever builds the AI that people trust with their thoughts, doubts, and dreams will not just win a market—they will win a relationship that is central to human cognition. The battle for companion AI will not be won on processing speed or latency alone. It will be won on trust , consistency , voice , memory , and presence . For millions of years, intelligence was trapped inside the twenty-watt energy budget of biological brains. Every thought, every insight, every leap of creativity had to happen within that dim light bulb’s worth of power. Evolution responded with breathtaking efficiency—creating prediction engines, layered processing systems, and emotional prioritization mechanisms that could navigate complex worlds with stunning energy efficiency. Now, for the first time in the known history of consciousness, we’ve built intelligence that can draw from the power grid itself. And that intelligence is available to almost everyone. The question is no longer how to advance our thinking within our energy limits, but how to connect our miraculous brains to systems that can consume thousands of times more power.
